went delayed ACLR (performed >8 weeks after injury).26 No significant differences
in postoperative knee ROM were found between the 2 groups.26 Additionally, one
recent study showed comparable patient-reported outcomes, with significant im-
provements in all subscales of the Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score
(KOOS) and favorable return rate to preinjury Tegner activity level after both early
and delayed ACLR.17 Notably, a high proportion of patients in both the early and
delayed ACLR groups were able to return to Tegner activity level 6 or higher, suggest-
ing surgical timing may have a limited influence on the rate of return to sport.17 Further-
more, objective International Knee Documentation Committee scores were shown to
be similar among patient groups, with the majority of (82% vs 71%, respectively) of
patients having grade AB pivot shift at the 12-month postoperative follow-up, indica-
tive of restored knee laxity because of both early and delayed ACLR.17
  Further research showed that patients with early, hamstring tendon ACLR achieve
superior outcomes in terms of postoperative isokinetic knee flexion strength after
2 years compared with patients who underwent delayed ACLR.27 Specifically, patients
with early surgery achieved significantly greater improvement in flexor strength at 180
(8.1% improvement) and 240 (9.4% improvement) per second, without significant
improvement in extensor strength.27 In the same study, early ACLR was associated
with fewer sick-leave days and decreased socioeconomic costs compared with
delayed ACLR.27 Consequently, while both early and delayed surgery seem to yield
good to excellent functional outcomes, a combination of functional outcomes should
SUMMARY

In light of the current evidence, an improved understanding of surgical timing is war-
ranted to optimize patient outcomes with ACLR in the setting of isolated ACL and
MLKIs. Although interpretation of the existing data is hampered by inconsistent defi-
nitions of surgical timing, early ACLR performed within weeks of injury may result in
equivalent to superior clinical and functional outcomes. Importantly, early ACLR
seems to be beneficial for decreasing the incidence of medial meniscus and chondral
injury by avoiding prolonged knee instability, with excellent clinical and functional out-
comes and no marked increase in the risk of postoperative arthrofibrosis compared
with delayed surgery. Future studies are required to clarify the cutoff between early
and delayed surgeries to determine the influence of concurrent surgical procedures
on optimal surgical timing and to explore the role of surgical timing in the treatment
of patients with MLKIs.

{

 "sourceFile": "Timing of anterior cruciate ligament surgery.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text, 'Timing of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Surgery' (Clin Sports Med, 2023), matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Rehabilitation", "Athletic Training"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Injured Athletes", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Narrative review in Clinics in Sports Medicine that critically assesses the literature on early versus delayed ACL reconstruction, including its effect on knee injuries, function, return to sport and cost. No search method is described; the review draws on prior systematic reviews, meta-analyses and randomised trials cited by the authors. The authors conclude that early reconstruction within weeks of injury may give equivalent or superior clinical and functional outcomes, and reduces medial meniscus and chondral injury.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The review has no described search, so the evidence is selected by the authors. The main limitation the authors identify is inconsistent definitions of early and delayed surgery across studies, which makes pooled interpretation hard.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the paper as settling the best time to operate for every athlete, when the authors say the cut-off between early and delayed surgery is still unclear and that the evidence for multiligament injuries is inconclusive.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2023,
   "citation": "Zsidai B, Kaarre J, Narup E, Samuelsson K. Timing of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Surgery. Clin Sports Med. 2023.",
   "doi": "10.1016/j.csm.2023.08.002",
   "abstract": "Narrative review of early versus delayed ACL reconstruction, covering definitions of timing, associated meniscus and cartilage injury, functional and patient-reported outcomes, return to sport and cost.",
   "tldr": "Early ACL reconstruction within weeks of injury appears at least as good as delayed surgery for function and outcomes, and may reduce further meniscus and cartilage damage. The exact cut-off between early and delayed surgery is still unclear.",
   "methods": "Narrative review. The aim was to critically assess the literature on surgical timing for ACL injury across postoperative outcomes. No search strategy, inclusion criteria or risk-of-bias method is described.",
   "findings": "The authors report that early ACL reconstruction was equivalent or superior to delayed reconstruction for clinical outcomes, subjective knee function and cost-effectiveness. Early surgery was associated with less intra-articular injury between injury and surgery, and in one cited study with greater flexor strength at 2 years. A cited study found similar return to Tegner level 6 or higher after early and delayed surgery, suggesting timing has a limited effect on return to sport rate.",
   "limitations": "The authors note that definitions of early and delayed ACL reconstruction vary widely, from days to months and from weeks to years, which limits comparison across studies. Future studies are needed to set the cut-off and to address multiligament knee injuries.",
   "practicalImplications": "Early reconstruction within weeks of injury may be considered in the setting of isolated ACL tears because it appears to be at least as good for function and may reduce meniscus and cartilage damage. The timing cut-off and the effect in multiligament injuries are not yet established.",
   "athleteDev": "Performance Application: the paper gives no performance outcome data. It supports timing surgery early when the goal is preserving the joint, but the review does not show a performance advantage.",
   "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: the cited evidence suggests a similar proportion of athletes return to Tegner level 6 or higher after early or delayed surgery, so timing alone should not be used to predict return to sport. The review does not give return-to-sport timeframes or criteria."
 }
}

Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery
https://doi.org/10.1007/s00402-021-03854-8

  ARTHROSCOPY AND SPORTS MEDICINE



Timing return‑to‑competition: a prospective registration of 45
different types of severe injuries in Germany’s highest football league
Werner Krutsch1,2 · Clemens Memmel3 · Volker Alt1 · Volker Krutsch4 · Tobias Tröß5 · Karen aus der Fünten5 ·
Tim Meyer5

Received: 17 December 2020 / Accepted: 2 March 2021
© The Author(s) 2021


Abstract
Introduction Many professional football players sustain at least one severe injury over the course of their career. Because
detailed epidemiological data on different severe injuries in professional football have been missing so far, this study describes
the frequency and return-to-competition (RTC) periods of different types of severe football injuries.
Material and methods This epidemiological investigation is a prospective standardised injury analysis based on national
media longitudinal registration. Injuries were classified according to the consensus statement by Fuller et al. (2006). The
analysis includes injuries sustained by players of the first German football league during the seasons 2014–2015 to 2017–
2018. Level of evidence: II.
Results Overall, 660 severe injuries were registered during the four seasons (mean 165 per season; 9.2 per season per team;
incidence in 1000 h: 0.77). The body region most frequently affected by severe injury was the knee (30.0%; 49.5 injuries per
season/SD 13.2) followed by the thigh (26.4%; 43.5 injuries/SD 4.2) and the ankle (16.7%; 27.5 injuries/SD 5.0). The distri-
bution of injuries over the course of a season showed a trend for ACL ruptures to mainly occur at the beginning of a season
(45.8%), overuse syndromes such as achillodynia (40.9%) and irritation of the knee (44.4%) during the winter months and
severe muscle and ankle injuries at the end of a season. ACL ruptures showed the longest RTC durations (median 222 days).
Conclusion This study presents detailed epidemiological data on severe injuries in professional football. The body region
most frequently affected by severe injuries was the knee. Several types of severe injuries showed a seasonal injury pattern.
The appropriate timing of RTC after an injury is one of the most important and complex decisions to be made. This study
provides information on the typical time loss due to specific severe football injuries, which may serve as a guideline.

Keywords Severe injury · Professional · Soccer · Return-to-competition · Epidemiology · Media-based

Timing return‑to‑competition: a prospective registration of 45
different types of severe injuries in Germany’s highest football league
Werner Krutsch1,2 · Clemens Memmel3 · Volker Alt1 · Volker Krutsch4 · Tobias Tröß5 · Karen aus der Fünten5 ·
Tim Meyer5

Received: 17 December 2020 / Accepted: 2 March 2021
© The Author(s) 2021


Abstract
Introduction Many professional football players sustain at least one severe injury over the course of their career. Because
detailed epidemiological data on different severe injuries in professional football have been missing so far, this study describes
the frequency and return-to-competition (RTC) periods of different types of severe football injuries.
Material and methods This epidemiological investigation is a prospective standardised injury analysis based on national
media longitudinal registration. Injuries were classified according to the consensus statement by Fuller et al. (2006). The
analysis includes injuries sustained by players of the first German football league during the seasons 2014–2015 to 2017–
2018. Level of evidence: II.
Results Overall, 660 severe injuries were registered during the four seasons (mean 165 per season; 9.2 per season per team;
incidence in 1000 h: 0.77). The body region most frequently affected by severe injury was the knee (30.0%; 49.5 injuries per
season/SD 13.2) followed by the thigh (26.4%; 43.5 injuries/SD 4.2) and the ankle (16.7%; 27.5 injuries/SD 5.0). The distri-
bution of injuries over the course of a season showed a trend for ACL ruptures to mainly occur at the beginning of a season
(45.8%), overuse syndromes such as achillodynia (40.9%) and irritation of the knee (44.4%) during the winter months and
severe muscle and ankle injuries at the end of a season. ACL ruptures showed the longest RTC durations (median 222 days).
Conclusion This study presents detailed epidemiological data on severe injuries in professional football. The body region
most frequently affected by severe injuries was the knee. Several types of severe injuries showed a seasonal injury pattern.
The appropriate timing of RTC after an injury is one of the most important and complex decisions to be made. This study
provides information on the typical time loss due to specific severe football injuries, which may serve as a guideline.

 "id": "Q71",
 "sourceFile": "Timing-based strategies to minimize the impact of long-haul travel on sleep - A pilot study in elite athletes traveling for competition.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",

 "identityCheck": "Title in text, 'Timing-based strategies to minimize the impact of long-haul travel on sleep: A pilot study in elite athletes traveling for competition', matches the filename.",

 "studyDesign": "Other",

 "audiences": ["Performance", "Athletic Training", "Coaching"],

 "evidenceSummary": "Pilot study in 10 national-level Canadian short-track speed skaters travelling to a World Cup in Beijing (13 time zones), who followed a tailored timing-based sleep schedule on arrival and in the days before competition. Total sleep time in Beijing did not differ from Canada or pre-season, was lower the night before the flight, and was about 10 minutes per night longer than a historical no-intervention dataset. Overall race rank was not affected by travel (p = 0.74).",
 "screeningLimitations": "Ten athletes, with no control group in the same competition, and the comparison is with a separate earlier dataset. Circadian phase and subjective jet lag were not measured, so the study cannot show how far the body clock shifted.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the timing schedule as having improved sleep and performance, when the performance result was not a comparison against a control and the authors describe the findings as preliminary.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2025,
   "citation": "Varesco G, Renaud-Roy A, Bieuzen F, Pattyn N, Simonelli G. Timing-based strategies to minimize the impact of long-haul travel on sleep: A pilot study in elite athletes traveling for competition. Physiol Rep. 2025;13:e70654.",
   "doi": "10.14814/phy2.70654",
   "abstract": "Ten national-level Canadian speed skaters followed a tailored sleep timing schedule before a World Cup in Beijing (13 time zones). Sleep in Beijing was compared with Canada and pre-season, and with an earlier dataset without intervention.",
   "tldr": "A tailored sleep timing plan kept total sleep in Beijing close to home and pre-season levels, and was linked with later bedtimes and slightly longer sleep compared with an earlier group. Race rank was not affected by travel in this small pilot.",
   "methods": "Pilot study in 10 national-level short-track speed skaters at a World Cup in Beijing. Athletes followed a tailored sleep and timing schedule on arrival and in the days before competition. Actigraphic sleep was compared across Canada, Beijing and pre-season, and with a similar earlier dataset without intervention. Race rank was analysed across phases.",
   "findings": "Total sleep time in Beijing did not differ from Canada (p = 0.254) or pre-season (p = 0.999), and was lower the night before travel (p < 0.001). Compared with the no-intervention dataset, bedtime was delayed, wake-up was later and total sleep time was about 10 minutes per night longer. Overall rank showed no time effect (p = 0.74).",
   "limitations": "Small sample of 10 athletes and no control group at the competition. The comparison dataset is from a different earlier study. Circadian phase and subjective jet lag were not measured, and the authors note that the findings are preliminary and need confirmation in larger samples.",
   "practicalImplications": "A tailored timing plan may help athletes sleep closer to their normal pattern after long-haul travel, but the gains are small and need confirming. Sleep was lowest the night before the early flight, so that night needs planning.",
   "athleteDev": "Performance Application: the timing plan maintained sleep in competition and did not show a rank change, but the study is a 10-athlete pilot with no control. It can inform a trial of timing strategies for travel, not a guarantee of performance benefit.",
   "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: the study is about healthy elite athletes travelling for competition and does not address injury or return to sport."
 }
}

Review

Tired of ACL Injures: A Review of Methods and Outcomes of
Neuromuscular Fatigue as a Risk Factor for ACL Injuries
Joshua L. I. Taylor 1 and Timothy A. Burkhart 1,2, *

  1  Faculty of Kinesiology and Physical Education, University of Toronto, 55 Harbord St.,
  Toronto, ON M5S 2W6, Canada
  2  Division of Orthopaedic Surgery, University of Toronto, 55 Harbord St., Toronto, ON M5S 2W6, Canada
  *  Correspondence: timothy.burkhart@utoronto.ca


  Abstract: Background/Objectives: One potential risk factor that remains especially con-
  tentious in the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury literature is the role of neuromuscular
  fatigue in ACL injury risk. Therefore, the purposes of this review are (i) to present the
  research and practical concepts of lower extremity neuromuscular fatigue; and (ii) to review
  the literature relating to neuromuscular fatigue as an ACL injury risk factor and mechanism.
  Methods: A structured review was performed in the Medline database using a search
  strategy that included terms such as “anterior cruciate ligament injury” and “knee injuries”
  combined with terms such as “injury” and “fatigue”. Articles were included if they in-
  cluded young healthy participants (18–35) and made a comparison between non-fatigued
  and fatigued states that were assessed with at least one lower extremity biomechanical
  variable associated with ACL injury risk. Results: Overall, there were 67 studies included,
  accounting for 1440 participants (627 male and 813 female) across a variety of sports and
  activities. Of these, 53 (79%) reported a post-fatigue change in the kinematics, kinetics,
  neuromuscular, and/or other (e.g., proprioceptive) outcomes that indicate that the par-
  ticipants would be at an increased risk of an ACL injury. The most common argument
  against fatigue as a risk factor is that ACL injuries do not tend to occur later in a game
  or season, when it is assumed that athletes would be most fatigued. Conclusions: The
  evidence presented in this review suggests that localized neuromuscular fatigue is a risk
  factor, among multiple factors, for ACL injuries, providing another modifiable risk factor
  that should be considered when developing ACL injury risk reduction interventions.
Academic Editor: John Buckley

Search and Analysis Methods
  A structured approach to the literature search was taken to ensure that a thorough,
  broad, and representative sample of literature was collected and reviewed. The Medline
  database was searched on 23 June 2023, using a structured search strategy that included
  terms such as “anterior cruciate ligament injury” and “knee injuries” combined with terms
  such as “injury” and “fatigue”. Details of the full search strategy can be found in the
  Supplemental Materials. Initially, 577 articles were included (567 from the initial search
  and 10 after searching reference lists) with 30 duplicates removed (Figure 1). Articles were
  included if (1) they involved young healthy participants (18–35); (2) made a comparison
  between non-fatigued and fatigued states; (3) measured at least one lower extremity
  biomechanical variable associated with ACL injury risk; and ((4) was published within the
  last 30 years (after 1993). Articles were excluded if they (1) included pediatric participants;
  (2) studied participants post-ACLR; and/or (3) specifically studied runners with a focus on
  running biomechanics. Systematic reviews were also excluded. After screening, a total of
  60 articles were included for data extraction.
  Sample demographics, including the number of participants, age, and sex, were
  extracted, in addition to the activity level and/or the sport participation of the participants
  (Table 1). Methodological information was then extracted and summarized, which included
  the fatiguing protocol, the way in which fatigue was identified/assessed, and the tasks that
  were used to test the effect of fatigue on lower extremity biomechanics (Table 1).

  Table 1. Summary of the included studies detailing the demographics of the participants included,
  the methods used to induce and assess the inset of fatigue, and the tasks used to compare between
  pre-fatigue and fatigued conditions.
  quantification of neuromuscular fatigue.

  5. Conclusions
  ACL injury is a well-researched phenomenon that is complex and multi-factorial. The
  research related to the potential effect that fatigue has on ACL injuries remains a controver-
  sial topic, given the difficulties in defining, measuring, and inducing fatigue in a repeatable
  and standardized manner. While the research remains a controversial topic, localized
  neuromuscular fatigue is likely a risk factor, among multiple factors, for ACL injuries. This
  is another modifiable risk factor that should be considered when developing ACL injury
  risk reduction interventions. Although further work is needed to best identify how fatigue
  can be integrated into risk reduction and rehabilitation programs, introducing assessments
  of individuals in the fatigued state is a possible first step. Implementing controlled training
  while fatigued may also allow individuals to develop movement strategies in the fatigued
  state. Finally, including a focus on neuromuscular endurance training may improve an
  individual’s resiliency to the factors that induce fatigue (e.g., greater force-generating
  capacity prior to reaching the point of fatigue). Future work should also aim to develop
  standardized methods of defining, measuring, and inducing neuromuscular fatigue to
  address current limitations and move toward a consensus.
  halves of individual competitions (odds ratio = 0.43) or full seasons (odds ratio = 1.27),
  fatigue cannot be associated with these injuries. This theory has also been supported by
  other research groups who found that more ACL injuries occurred earlier in the season [99]
  or that the distribution of ACL injuries was not different across timepoints [100,101].
  However, a limitation of this approach is that none of these studies included a physiological
  measure of fatigue. While it would be a difficult task, experimentally, to collect in-game
  physiological and/or biomechanical data, recent advances in wearable technologies suggest
  that this may be feasible and should be explored in future research of this kind. Additionally,
  lower extremity neuromuscular fatigue can occur at any point within a shift, series, game,

 "evidenceSummary": "Structured review of MEDLINE (searched 23 June 2023) on whether localised neuromuscular fatigue is an ACL injury risk factor, limited to young healthy participants aged 18 to 35 comparing fatigued and non-fatigued states with a lower-limb biomechanical measure.  "paper": {

   "citation": "Taylor JLI, Burkhart TA. Tired of ACL Injures: A Review of Methods and Outcomes of Neuromuscular Fatigue as a Risk Factor for ACL Injuries. Biomechanics. 2025;5:11.",
   "doi": "10.3390/biomechanics5010011",
   "abstract": "Structured MEDLINE review of studies comparing fatigued and non-fatigued states in young healthy adults using lower-limb biomechanical measures linked to ACL injury risk. Most included studies reported changes consistent with higher ACL injury risk after fatigue.",
   "tldr": "Localised neuromuscular fatigue changed knee and hip movement and loading measures linked to ACL injury in most of the lab studies reviewed. Fatigue appears to be one risk factor among several, but the evidence is laboratory-based and the methods vary.",
   "methods": "Structured review of MEDLINE, searched 23 June 2023, with terms for ACL and knee injury combined with injury and fatigue. Eligible studies involved healthy participants aged 18 to 35, compared non-fatigued and fatigued states, and measured at least one lower-limb biomechanical variable linked to ACL risk. Studies after ACL reconstruction, in paediatric samples or on running biomechanics were excluded, as were systematic reviews. Sample data, fatigue protocols and outcome tasks were extracted.",
   "findings": "The authors report 67 included studies with 1440 participants (627 male, 813 female) across varied sports and activities. Of these, 53 (79%) reported a post-fatigue change in kinematics, kinetics, neuromuscular or proprioceptive outcomes indicating increased ACL injury risk. The authors note that competition-half and season comparisons found no effect of fatigue on injury, but that none of those studies measured fatigue physiologically.",
   "limitations": "The review does not include a formal risk-of-bias assessment or pooled analysis. Methods report 60 articles for data extraction, while the Results and Abstract report 67 studies, which the review does not reconcile. The included studies are laboratory biomechanics in healthy young adults, and fatigue was induced and measured with varying protocols, which the authors identify as a barrier to consensus.",
   "practicalImplications": "Localised fatigue may be considered as one modifiable risk factor when designing ACL injury prevention. Practitioners could assess movement in a fatigued state and train controlled movement while fatigued, alongside neuromuscular endurance work.",
   "athleteDev": "Performance Application: the review supports including fatigued-state movement assessment and endurance work in training, and the authors suggest this could help athletes keep control of landing and cutting when tired. The paper does not test a training programme.",
   "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: the review excludes post-ACL reconstruction participants, so it does not show how fatigue affects return to sport. Its suggestion to assess movement while fatigued is a prevention or rehabilitation idea that has not been tested in that setting."
 }
}

import json
p='Q67.json'
d=json.load(open(p))

The authors note many studies lacked the timing detail needed, and the abstract's ACL game-segment confidence interval (0.47 to 7.92) does not match the Results text (0.07 to 2.56)."
d['evidenceSummary']="Systematic review and meta-analysis of ACL, groin and hamstring injuries by time of season and game segment. Five databases were searched to November 2017, yielding 15 articles and 21 data sets after screening. Pooled odds ratios comparing the first and second halves of the season showed no difference for ACL (OR 1.27, 95% CI 0.43 to 3.78), groin (OR 1.79, 0.63 to 5.06) or hamstring (OR 1.16, 0.88 to 1.53) injuries. Game-segment analysis in the Results text also showed no difference for ACL (first vs second half OR 0.43, 95% CI 0.07 to 2.56; first vs fourth quarter OR 0.84, 0.22 to 2.68) or hamstring (first vs second half OR 0.85, 0.58 to 1.24) injuries."
d['paper']['citation']="Doyle TLA, Schilaty ND, Webster KE, Hewett TE. Time of Season and Game Segment Is Not Related to Likelihood of Lower-Limb Injuries: A Meta-Analysis. Clin J Sport Med. 2019."
d['paper']['findings']="Season, first half compared with second half: ACL OR 1.27 (95% CI 0.43 to 3.78), groin OR 1.79 (0.63 to 5.06), hamstring OR 1.16 (0.88 to 1.53). Game segment, first vs second half: ACL OR 0.43 (95% CI 0.07 to 2.56), hamstring OR 0.85 (0.58 to 1.24). Game segment, first vs fourth quarter: ACL OR 0.84 (0.22 to 2.68), hamstring OR 0.62 (0.34 to 1.16). The authors conclude that time in season or game does not influence ACL, groin or hamstring injury risk."
d['paper']['limitations']="Only 15 articles met criteria, with few data sets for ACL and a single study for the groin game-segment analysis. Injury counts were absolute and not normalised to exposure or minutes. The abstract gives the ACL game-segment confidence interval as 0.47 to 7.92, which does not match the Results text (0.07 to 2.56) and does not contain the point estimate of 0.43, so the Results value is reported here."
json.dump(d,open(p,'w'),ensure_ascii=False,indent=1)
print('ok')
EOF

import json
p='Q65.json'; d=json.load(open(p))

Effects were small and the authors note they are minor relative to measurement error, so the study does not show transfer to sport-specific performance."
json.dump(d,open(p,'w'),ensure_ascii=False,indent=1)

p='Q66.json'; d=json.load(open(p))
d['evidenceSummary']="Narrative review in Sports Medicine that argues for a shift in ACL injury management toward education, conservative management with surgery as needed, and rehabilitation tailored to return-to-sport goals. It discusses cited trials and reviews, including trials comparing home-based with physiotherapist-led rehabilitation after ACL reconstruction, which the authors report found no superiority of supervised rehabilitation. No search method is described."
d['screeningLimitations']="The paper is a narrative review with no described search, so the evidence base is selected by the authors. Much of the cited evidence concerns reconstruction rather than non-operative care, which the authors acknowledge has little research."
json.dump(d,open(p,'w'),ensure_ascii=False,indent=1)
print('ok')
EOF
